data.title: Who is Bahram Vakil, the founder of AZB, succeeding Noel Tata as Trent chairman
data.description:
The Tata Group is set for a leadership change at Trent Ltd, one of its key retail businesses. Bahram N Vakil is set to succeed Noel Tata as the company's chairman.

The appointments were approved during the board meeting on October 29. Vakil’s appointment marks a shift from a business leader associated with the expansion of the group's retail operations to a corporate lawyer with experience in financial restructuring, insolvency and project finance.

The transition comes amid differences between the Tata Sons board and Tata Trusts over the group's governance and control.

According to the company's stock exchange filing, Vakil will assume the chairmanship on November 12, a day after Noel Tata steps down from the position. Noel Tata will retire as chairman and director at the close of business on November 11, following nearly 29 years of association with Trent. He will continue his association with the company as chairman emeritus.

Who Is Bahram Vakil?

Bahram Vakil is the co-founder of AZB & Partners, one of India's leading law firms. He has built his career in corporate law, restructuring, insolvency, infrastructure and project finance. He holds an LLM degree from Columbia University and is a member of the New York State Bar.

Vakil became part of the board of Tata Investment Corporation in March 2025, taking on the roles of vice-chairman and independent director. He was also reportedly considered for a position on the Tata Sons board during discussions over vacancies.

Over the course of his legal career, Vakil has advised distressed funds, insolvency professionals and domestic and international banks on restructuring and bankruptcy matters. He has also worked on large stressed accounts referred by the Reserve Bank of India for insolvency proceedings.

In 2023, Vakil served on the Insolvency Law Academy's Thought Committee on Bank Insolvency and was also part of an expert committee formed to recommend changes to arbitration law. He also chaired ASSOCHAM's National Council on Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and Valuation that year. Vakil has also been recognised by international legal publications for his work in restructuring and project finance.

Noel Tata Stepping Down

Noel Tata will step down as chairman and director of Trent on November 11, after nearly three decades with the company. The board approved the transition at its meeting on October 29, in accordance with the Tata Group's governance guidelines relating to board composition and director retirement.

Noel Tata has been associated with Trent since 1997 and played a key role in the company's growth and expansion in India's retail sector. In its exchange filing, the company said his leadership had helped Trent achieve important milestones, strengthen its market position and deliver sustained growth for stakeholders.

data.title: Markets Espresso: The whole thing is that ki Bhaiyya...Sabse bada Rupaiyaa
data.description:
Tumko maloom hai ki yeh ek paisa kya hota hai? Ek-Ek paisa jama karo to ek rupya banta hai. Ek-Ek rupya jama karo to 100 banta hai, 100 jama karo to hazaar banta hai. Hazaar hazaar jama karo to lakh aur lakh se crore banta hai. Yeh ek paisa, ek crore ka beej hai. Jo aadmi beej ki parvah nahi karega, wo na to fasal uga sakta hai, na phal pa sakta hai!

Hello Espresso Lovers! We are back after what felt like a never-ending week with over 200 results and a barrage of developments besides them. You may wonder why I would begin with the late Kadar Khan's memorable lines from Dariya Dil (1987) before greeting you all? The lines may be a message to companies in a land far, far away that have embarked on incessant, eye-watering spending plans without any assurance that any of it will even return to them. And finally, it seems the investor community has started to take note and feel worried.

Perhaps this one meme is central to the entire episode of today. This is the question investors are finally beginning to ask the Magnificent Seven companies as they keep reporting their results. Just last year, the situation was the complete opposite. The more these companies spent, the bigger the capex guidance they announced, the faster the stocks ran. Investors thought the money spent would return faster than an answer generated by AI when given a prompt. Alas, that was not the case.

For a better part of this year, the spending plans were largely viewed positively as companies assured investors that this was being done only through their own internal cash flows. But then came debt. And then some more. Investors thought, okay, they are still generating enough cash to repay the debt. They'll be fine. But when this spending binge began to show up in their results, the warning signs began to flash, the proverbial Khatre ki ghanti began to ring, and investors began to ask questions they should have asked a lot earlier - Will this money ever return?

Take a look at Alphabet - Google's parent. For the first time in four years, its results missed expectations. In an ideal case scenario, investors would cut them some slack and say, it's alright, the law of averages would have caught up someday. But no. There was a bigger devil in the detail. Its free cash flow was negative for the second quarter in a row. Not just that, it was almost 4.5x higher than what analysts had anticipated. The result? Stock falls 13%, the most in a single day since its IPO way back in 2004. $500 billion of market value wiped out in a single day. Worse still, they plan on spending more next year - $300 billion!

And Alphabet is not a stray incident. Most of the big tech companies that have reported results so far have reported negative free cash flows this quarter. Meta reported one for the first time after listing this quarter, and the stock was duly punished by investors for it as well. The same is the case with Amazon - negative free cash flow of $7 billion in the same quarter last year. This time? Wait for it...negative $42 billion. The only one that stood out? Microsoft. Still reported positive FCF even though it dropped 27% from last year. The question is, for how long it remains in positive territory if spending continues the way it has been.

And then comes Intel. The perfect synonym for "dead-man walking" for a better part of this year. Once a legend, almost driven to the border of irrelevance, administration picks up stake, things start looking up, stock runs, and runs hard. Gains almost 250% in just 7-8 months. Then comes the moment of truth. Numbers. Weaker than estimates. In fact, way weaker. Guidance disappoints. The Israel factory incident drags a $600 million hit over the next two quarters.

When a stock that has not done much disappoints, the investors choose to look away. But when you run faster than your legs can take, the fall is steeper, deeper, and more brutal. A 29% drop on Friday, the worst day since the 1970s. That's one-third of your value gone in a matter of hours. The biggest loser? No. Not retail for a change. DONALD TRUMP! His administration's stake took a $12 billion hit as a result of this fall. Wonder what he has to say on Truth Social about this, since he has gloated enough and more about Intel's stock returns.

We brought this to you last week. The highlight of every earnings season. But this time around, there's something different. Usually, when a stock would deliver good/bad numbers, the reaction to it would be limited to a day, max two. This time around, stocks with good numbers have continued to move higher, while those with bad ones have just not stopped correcting.

Ather Energy is the best example of this. The stock had corrected 20% to 25% from its previous highs, due to routine profit booking. Then came the results. First-ever profit. Not just EBITDA, but PAT level as well. Add to that some capacity expansion plans and strong management commentary. The street was as joyous as it could be. A 27% move last week on the upside, the best performer on the Nifty 500, and back at new highs as well!

On the flip side, there is CarTrade Tech - the potential "wild child" of the market. A ₹1,600 IPO falls to ₹350, then goes back to ₹3,000 plus, and then falls from there again. For a company growing between 20% and 30% every quarter, a 10% growth quarter was difficult to digest for the market. Yes, the festive season shifted compared to the base quarter, but 10% was just not acceptable to the street. The result? Down 23% this week, the worst Nifty 500 performer, now down 35% from those very highs that it had surged to and made the market sit up and take note.

Financial educator, speaker and author, Alan Miltz gave a very popular quote: "Revenue is vanity, profit is sanity, and cash is king!" Right now, the big techs are showing complete disregard for the same King that once gave them the trillion-dollar crowns they now sit on. Majrooh Saab (the great late Majrooh Sultanpuri) was not a visionary for no reason that he wrote Sabse Bada Rupaiyaa all the way back in 1976, and those lines hold true more than ever 50 years later! The whole thing is that ki Bhaiyya… sabse bada rupaiyaa!

Festivities begin for Diwali next week - the festival of lights and from all of us at CNBC-TV18, we wish you all a happy, prosperous and joyous Diwali and New Year. We are only grateful for your love, appreciation and feedback, and we hope that the festival brings plenty of light to your lives and the new year turns out to be a lot better than what this one has been! We'll see you next week with the latest brew! Happy Diwali to one and all!

data.title: India aims to be globally competitive semiconductor powerhouse by 2047: MoD
data.description:
India aspires to emerge as a globally competitive, dependable and technologically self-reliant semiconductor powerhouse by 2047, with leadership in selected next-generation chip technologies, the defence ministry said on Friday.

The vision encompasses the development of a vibrant and sustainable semiconductor ecosystem, generation of high-value employment opportunities and delivery of inclusive societal benefits, it said.

The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) participated in the Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave (ESTIC) 2026 at the Bharat Mandapam from October 27-29.

Inaugurated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the conclave with the theme ‘Creative Minds, Catalysing Science, Empowering Society’ was jointly organised by 12 ministries and departments under the guidance of the principal scientific adviser to the government of India, the ministry said in a statement.

The event showcased cutting-edge research, deep-tech breakthroughs, and thought-provoking discussions with Nobel laureates, global experts, policymakers and emerging leaders, igniting a new era of scientific leadership, it said.

The DRDO, as one of the key organisers, led the thematic session on ‘Semiconductors & Next-Generation Chips’.

Chaired by B K Das, Director General, Electronics and Communication Systems (ECS), the session brought together eminent leaders from the industry, academia, indigenous chip-development ecosystem and defence electronics.

“The discussions explored emerging developments in semiconductor technologies, purpose-built artificial intelligence (AI) system-on-chips (SoCs), intelligence at the silicon edge and the evolving microprocessor landscape, the statement said.

The session also highlighted DRDO's evolving role in enabling industries and startups to develop game-changing solutions, accelerate next-generation chip design and strengthen indigenous core technologies.

“India aspires to emerge as a globally competitive, dependable and technologically self-reliant semiconductor powerhouse by 2047, with leadership in selected next-generation chip technologies,” the ministry said.

The DRDO outreach stall at ESTIC 2026 showcased key initiatives, achievements, research programmes and contributions of the ministry towards science, technology and innovation.

It featured a diverse range of indigenous technologies developed by DRDO laboratories, including advanced communication systems, quantum technology prototypes, extreme-cold-weather clothing, PRABALA female full-body protector, passive and powered exoskeletons, portable hybrid energy management systems, high-power pulse laser diodes and scramjet engine technology, the statement said.

Semiconductor technology is a critical enabler of national sovereignty, economic strength and digital security. It plays a key role in advancing the vision of Viksit Bharat by 2047 and Aatmanirbhar Bharat by strengthening indigenous technological capabilities, the ministry said.

From communication devices and advanced sensing systems to sophisticated defence platforms, semiconductor chips determine the performance, efficiency and reliability of modern technologies.

Beyond chip manufacturing, technological self-reliance requires comprehensive capabilities in chip design, fabrication, testing, industrial-scale production and resilient supply chains, it said.

He also brings substantial expertise in domestic and international resource mobilisation, strategic treasury management, corporate finance, taxation and legal affairs, project appraisal and monitoring, lending operations, loan recovery and stressed asset management.

Nayak holds a Master’s degree in Commerce from Utkal University, Bhubaneswar, Odisha. He is a fellow member of the Institute of Cost and Management Accountants of India and a qualified Company Secretary.

His appointment had been earlier approved by Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC).

data.title: "We don't rely on just one face": Sachin Pilot rejects rivalry charge in Punjab Congress
data.description:
New Delhi, Oct. 31 -- With the 2027 Punjab Assembly Elections nearing, Congress general secretary and state in-charge Sachin Pilot on Saturday said that said the party did not depend on a handful of individuals to lead the campaign in the state.

In an exclusive interview with ANI, Pilot said the party had no shortage of experienced people capable of running a state. As with the long history of Congress, new faces emerge from every corner of the country to be in leadership positions.

"Our party doesn't depend on just one, two, or five leaders. Ours is a 140-year-old party with presence in every single village. When new saplings are planted, new flowers bloom, new leaders emerge, and fresh leadership is born. That's the way life works," Pilot said.

When asked about internal rivalry due to strong political leaders in a single party, Pilot rejected the charge. "There is no rivalry; it is healthy competition," the Congress leader told ANI.

Referring to Punjab Congress chief Pargat Singh, he emphasised that Congress does not rely on a single strong leader but rather a team which helps with achieving the party's goals.

"We don't rely on just one face; our entire team is contesting together. Our new state president comes from a sports background. A captain is strong, but a captain is only as strong as the team backing him," he said.

Instead Pilot has said that it is the Bharatiya Janata Party which is facing rivalry within the party, claiming that former Punjab BJP president Captain Amrinder Singh is 'unhappy' after leaving the Congress fold.

Asked about who would be the chief ministerial face, Pilot said, "When in government, the sitting CM naturally leads the campaign. In opposition, across all states, the leadership comes collectively from the Leader of Opposition, the state party president, and top senior leaders, and we have many."

The comments come in the backdrop of the party earlier facing speculation regarding a rift within the party. Former Punjab Congress chief Amarinder Singh Raja Warring claimed that AICC state in-charge Sachin Pilot may have decided that it was time to remove 'Raja' from the post.

"Given my long journey in politics, I feel that Sachin Pilot must have decided it was time to remove 'Raja' from the post. I don't have concrete proof of this, but perhaps the General Secretary felt that Raja should be removed," Warring had said back in October 2.

Similarly, there was speculation regarding Charanjit Singh Channi too, where the former CM's supporters were repeatedly raising slogans in support of Channi.

Contrasting Congress with the ruling AAP government, he said, "AAP has only one Chief Minister face; nobody even knows who the rest are. We have immense depth," he said.

Pilot voiced pride in the party's grassroots leaders, highlighting their deep roots and widespread popular appeal.

"No, they are all deeply rooted grassroots leaders with widespread popularity. I am proud to have that. If we didn't have that and had only one or two faces, that would be a problem. Across different districts, we have numerous leaders who have served as MLAs, MPs, ministers, CM, and Deputy CM," he said.

Asked whether the exit of leaders with personal followings, such as Captain Amarinder Singh, hurts the party, Pilot spoke warmly of the former chief minister but called his move a personal decision. He claimed that Captain Amarinder Singh's statements show that he is unhappy even after joining the BJP.

"On a personal level, Captain Amarinder Singh is a very pleasant gentleman. But he chose to join another party; that was his personal call. Even there, he isn't very happy, and his own statements reflect that. In the BJP, newcomers rarely get genuine respect. The reality is that most prominent BJP figures in Punjab today are former Congressmen. They have hardly any homegrown presence," he said.

On whether the departures would affect the Congress, Pilot said, "I don't think it will have much of an impact. Naturally, whenever anyone leaves a party, it's not good... nobody wants to lose a member of the team. As for others, some leave under pressure, someone faces legal cases, or someone faces raids, so people sometimes give in."

On whether it was a point of no return for the former chief minister, he said, "Unfortunately, that is a question I cannot answer for you. But as far as I am concerned, I have had no personal contact or conversation with Captain Amarinder Singh."

He framed the upcoming elections as a direct fight between the Congress and the ruling Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), accusing the state government of failing on law and order, drugs and the economy.

Pilot said the AAP government had squandered the massive mandate it received in 2021.

"There are 117 assembly seats there, and people gave 92 seats to the Aam Aadmi Party. A historic win. I think that huge mandate was frittered away," he said.

Pilot accused the government of failing on every parameter, including crime, drugs, gangsters, extortion, investment and job creation.

Painting a grave picture of the drug problem in Punjab, he said he had travelled extensively across the state recently. "If you sit at home or in a village, ordering food via Blinkit or Zomato takes 45 minutes, whereas 'chitta' and drugs reach your doorstep in 20 minutes. Home delivery of drugs," he claimed.

Broadening his attack, Pilot accused the Centre of failing to stop drones and illegal drugs and arms from crossing the border, but maintained that their spread within Punjab could not happen without local involvement. "The systematic manner in which it spreads to every village cannot happen without the connivance of the local police, administration, and the political establishment," he said.

Pilot acknowledged that the situation had existed under Congress as well, but said that the situation had worsened significantly. "It was there, but it has now become 10 times worse," he said.

Pilot linked drugs to a wider chain of crime. He said drug money feeds illegal arms, which in turn sustain gangs that run extortion rackets, some of them directly from prison cells. He said society was once again under severe distress, reminiscent of the 1980s.

He also pointed to the state's finances, claiming Punjab's debt had climbed to Rs.4.5 lakh crore from Rs.2.5 lakh crore. "No investments are coming in, talent is fleeing the state, and drugs have severely weakened the social fabric," he said.

On extortion, Pilot said traders receive ransom calls from abroad and are too afraid to report them. "I have personally visited dozens of homes where people lost their lives simply because they couldn't afford to pay or refused to pay," he said.

He accused the AAP government of having a single agenda: "to promote, protect, and propagate their own leaders using taxpayers' money." Recalling Punjab's legacy of the Green Revolution and White Revolution, he said the Congress wanted to restore the state to its glory days.

Asked who would lead the Congress, given that several senior leaders and former chief ministers have joined the BJP, Pilot said the party did not depend on a few individuals. He described the Congress as a 140-year-old party present in every village, where new leadership constantly emerges.

"We don't rely on just one face; our entire team is contesting together," he said, adding that the new state president comes from a sports background. "A captain is strong, but a captain is only as strong as the team backing him."

Pressed on who would be the chief ministerial face, Pilot said that in opposition, leadership is collective, drawn from the Leader of Opposition, the state president and senior leaders. He said AAP had only one face, while the Congress had deep bench strength. Denying that this created rivalry, he called it "healthy competition," saying the party has many grassroots leaders who have served as MLAs, MPs, ministers, chief minister and deputy chief minister.

Pilot described former chief minister Captain Amarinder Singh as "a very pleasant gentleman" but said joining the BJP was his personal decision. He claimed newcomers rarely get genuine respect in the BJP and that most of its prominent Punjab faces are former Congress members.

Asked about possible back-channel talks for Amarinder's return, Pilot said he had had no conversation with him. On whether it was a point of no return, he said he could not answer. He said that when leaders leave, "it's not good," but added that some leave under pressure from legal cases or raids.

Responding to speculation about an Akali Dal-BJP alliance, Pilot said the Congress's direct contest was with AAP. Pilot said the Congress vote bank was "rock solid" across Doaba, Majha and Malwa. He argued that voters want a stable government and would not waste votes on parties unable to form one.

"People cast their vote for a stable, lasting government. For that, there are only two viable options," he said, adding that AAP had asked for "one chance" and betrayed voters. "Now, the public wants change."

The parties are gearing up for the 2027 Punjab Assembly elections. In the 2022 elections, AAP won the polls with 92 of 117 seats, while Congress, which is eyeing a comeback, won 18 seats.

data.title: Capillary Technologies fraud: KPMG finds impersonation likely behind 3-million-euro loss at Czech unit
data.description:
Impersonation, not hacking, most likely cost Capillary Technologies’ Czech subsidiary more than €3 million, a forensic report by KPMG has found, according to the company's exchange filing on Saturday, October 31.

The company shared a summary of the findings that cost its Czech subsidary 3,041,169.90 euros on the exchanges on Saturday.

What KPMG found?

KPMG said the evidence was “most consistent with” a payment-diversion fraud built on impersonation of executives and legal professionals, social engineering, a lookalike web domain and off-channel messages. It found no sign that malware, a compromised mailbox or email spoofing caused the payments.

Session M Czech Republic s.r.o., a step-down subsidiary of Capillary, made four payments abroad between June 26 and July 2, this year. Capillary had announced a KPMG investigation into a “cyber-enabled banking fraud” on July 31.

What happened Then?

The fraudsters convinced staff that Capillary was planning a confidential, time-sensitive acquisition. They backed the claim with a non-disclosure agreement, invoices, payment requests, bank details and payment confirmations. They also used WhatsApp and personal email, which, KPMG said, reduced the company’s visibility of the exchanges.

The report said the emails came from law-ogier.co.uk, which was designed to be a working lookalike of the legitimate ogier.com domain. KPMG said in the report that it had found no traditional spoofing, and the messages passed standard sender checks known as SPF and DKIM. It further said that passing such checks does not prove a sender or payment instruction is genuine.

KPMG, however, could neither prove nor rule out claims that deepfake voice or video was used. It had no original audio, video or call data, and did not examine the personal phones used for WhatsApp, according to the filing.

Three payments went to ZZDJB CO LIMITED at HSBC Hong Kong whilw another one went to ZHONGXIAN TRADING PTE. LTD at UOB Singapore. Tracing the money beyond these first accounts, identifying the owners or recovering it fell outside the scope of the review the filing said.

KPMG did not name an individual or group behind the fraud.

The report further noted that KPMG also lacked bank-portal approval logs, Slack records and complete network data, so it could not independently check how the payments were approved.

KPMG noted that the absence of compromise in the records it reviewed was not proof that none occurred, and the report did not establish how the fraudsters learned the company’s approval patterns.

How Have Capillary Technologies Shares Performed?

The shares of Capillary Technologies ended 3.4% lower at the end of trade on Friday October 30, extending the company's loses for the third straight session. The stock ended at ₹504, well below its IPO price of ₹577, having made its stock market debut last year. The stock is down 25% so far for the year.

data.title: SEBI imposes ₹1 crore fine on CDSL for multiple compliance lapses
data.description:
Market regulator SEBI on Friday imposed a penalty of ₹1 crore on Central Depository Services (India) Ltd (CDSL) for multiple compliance lapses, including failure to communicate reasons for rejection of pledge requests to the depository participants (DPs) of both the pledgor and pledgee and shortcomings in disaster recovery drills.

CDSL has been directed to pay the penalty within 45 days, failing which recovery proceedings may be initiated.

In its 102-page order, SEBI said CDSL had violated several regulatory requirements during FY2023-24, following an inspection of its operations.

The violations included failure to communicate reasons for rejection of pledge requests to the depository participants of both the pledgor and pledgee, non-compliance with prescribed procedures for handling Client Unpaid Securities Accounts (CUSA), inadequate measures to prevent unauthorised data transmission and shortcomings in disaster recovery operations.

The regulator also found that CDSL had failed to patch identified vulnerabilities within the timeline prescribed by SEBI.

Further, its Vulnerability Assessment and Penetration Testing (VAPT) exercise was not comprehensive as it did not cover all domains and external applications.

"Noticee (CDSL) has been found to have committed multiple compliance lapses in the discharge of its depository functions. These include failure to communicate the reasons for rejection of pledge requests to the DPs of the pledgor and pledgee, non-adherence to the joint proposal framed ...in relation to CUSA operations, inadequate measures to prevent unauthorised transmission of data, incomplete migration of operations to the DR site during the DR drill, failure to patch vulnerabilities within the timeline stipulated by SEBI, and conducting a VAPT exercise that was not comprehensive," SEBI said.

SEBI observed that the lapses directly impinged upon CDSL's core obligations as a depository, which provides the foundational, system -- critical physical and digital infrastructure for electronic record-keeping, dematerialisation and ownership transfers.

"Given the systemic importance of a depository, such deficiencies have implications not only for individual investors but also for the integrity and stability of the Indian securities market," SEBI said, adding that the violations were serious in nature and warranted appropriate regulatory action.

Consequently, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has imposed a penalty of ₹1 crore on the depository.

The regulator, however, said the remedial measures subsequently undertaken by CDSL had been duly considered.

In July, the regulator imposed a penalty of ₹1 crore on CDSL for cybersecurity lapses linked to the malware attack that disrupted its systems in November 2022.

data.title: Ansem Says Time Is a Key Risk-Management Factor in Short-Term Trading
data.description: Crypto trader Ansem shared his approach to managing risk in short-term trades. According to ChainCatcher, he said traders should consider time—not just price and stop-loss levels—when assessing whether a trade is working. When he enters a trade, he expects a clear market move to develop quickly; if Bitcoin stays near his entry price for an extended period without moving as anticipated, he reassesses the trade. He may exit early if the expected move fails to materialize, even if his stop-loss has not been triggered. Ansem said short-term trading can help traders identify sooner whether a strategy is working, and that deciding whether to hold a trade should take into account how long the market takes to meet expectations as well as its price action.

data.title: "What's the hurry?": KTR questions IDBI Bank valuation, seeks answers from Centre over proposed sale
data.description:
Hyderabad, Oct. 31 -- BRS working president K T Rama Rao (KTR) has questioned the Union Government over the proposed sale of IDBI Bank, raising concerns about the bank's valuation, changes in the bidding process and the alleged failure to account for its valuable assets, including prime real estate in Hyderabad.

He has also sought answers on why the concerns raised by bank employees were not being addressed.

In a social media post, KTR said public sector undertakings (PSUs) and public sector banks were national assets that needed to be safeguarded.

Expressing concern over reports of alleged undervaluation of IDBI Bank, he questioned the rationale behind changing the rules and valuation methodology after the bids reportedly fell below the reserve price.

"Why were the rules and valuation methodology changed when bids fell below the reserve price?" he asked, seeking transparency in the disinvestment process.

KTR also drew attention to IDBI Bank's valuable real estate holdings, particularly prime land parcels in Hyderabad. He questioned whether the actual worth of these properties had been properly assessed and included in the overall valuation of the bank before proceeding with the proposed stake sale.

The BRS leader further questioned the Union Government's response to concerns expressed by IDBI Bank employees. He wanted to know why their objections and apprehensions were not being adequately addressed before taking a decision on the future of the public sector bank.

Emphasising that PSUs and public sector banks were national assets and needed to be protected, KTR said the Union Government owed the country clear answers before selling a reputed public sector bank to a private player.

He stressed the need for transparency and accountability in a transaction involving a major public sector banking institution and questioned the urgency behind the proposed sale.

Concluding his post with a pointed question to the Centre, KTR asked, "What's the hurry?"

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) had placed IDBI Bank under its Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework in May 2017 due to its deteriorating financial condition. The restrictions were lifted in March 2021 following improvements in the lender's financial performance.

The Union Cabinet on Wednesday (October 14) approved the sale of a controlling 60.72 per cent stake in IDBI Bank to Canada's Fairfax Financial Holdings for Rs 52,878 crore, following which Life Insurance Corporation of India's (LIC) shareholding will fall to 19 per cent.

The restructuring follows a significant improvement in IDBI Bank's financial health, with gross non-performing assets (GNPAs) declining from 31.78 per cent in September 2018 to 2.32 per cent in March 2026. Net non-performing assets (NNPAs) also fell sharply from 17.30 per cent to 0.15 per cent during the same period, while the bank posted a net profit of Rs 9,513 crore in FY26.

data.title: Best of the week | A bell, family and a Rs.13 trillion promise: the week Jio went public
data.description:
New Delhi, Oct. 31 -- Best of the Week is a weekly newsletter by Siddharth Sharma/Shravani Sinha. Subscribe to Mint's newsletters to get them directly in your inbox.

Some weeks, the market hands you a plot twist. This week, it handed you a family portrait.

On Wednesday morning, four generations of the Ambani family stood on stage at the National Stock Exchange as Jio Platforms Ltd stepped into public markets. Akash and Isha rang the bell at 10am. Mukesh Ambani, by all accounts, was moved to tears as his son Anant took the mic.

Anant put it the way only an Ambani could. For him, business is puja (worship), he said, and every puja ends with prasad. Today, Jio is shared with India. Isha spoke of a father who has found the courage, again and again, to build what others called impossible. Akash looked ahead: having democratized data in its first 10 years, Jio now wants to do the same for AI, cloud, connected devices and even connectivity from space.

Lovely speeches. But markets don't clap. They vote with money, and on Wednesday they voted loudly.

Jio opened at Rs.1,358, already 21% above its issue price. Then it kept climbing, closing at about Rs.1,417, up nearly 27%, on a day the Nifty slipped. By evening, Jio was worth around Rs.13 trillion, making it India's second-most valuable company, behind only parent Reliance Industries Ltd.

There was a juicy sub-plot, too. Listed Reliance companies together crossed Rs.30 trillion, while listed Tata companies stood at Rs.25.3 trillion. Reliance is now India's most valuable listed conglomerate, a crown the Tata Group had held until now.

Why does that matter beyond bragging rights? Because India's mega-IPOs have a habit of disappointing on day one. Mint's analysis found that none of the five biggest issues before Jio gained more than 2% on debut, and three ended below their offer price. Jio walked straight past that jinx. History also warns that a strong start isn't a finish. Reliance Power Ltd opened 21.7% above its offer price and still closed at a 17.2% discount. Coal India Ltd went the other way, widening its gains.

Two days after the bell, Jio reported its September quarter earnings on Friday, after market hours. It was its first report card as a listed company, and it delivered steady growth, backed by continued subscriber additions, growing traction in home broadband and sustained momentum in digital services.

Net profit came in at Rs.8,389 crore, up 13.7% from the same quarter last year and 8% from the previous quarter. Revenue from operations rose to Rs.40,475 crore, up 11.4% year-on-year and 3.3% sequentially. Jio credited subscriber additions, organic per-user growth and expansion in digital services.

For context, the June quarter had seen revenue of Rs.39,173 crore, up 2.4% sequentially and 12% on-year. Net profit was Rs.7,764 crore, up 9.2% on-year, though it had slipped 2.15% from the quarter before. The stock ended Friday 1.1% higher at Rs.1,437.50, ahead of the results.

Without a tariff hike, Jio's per-user growth from one quarter to the next has stayed largely flat for the past few quarters, and promotional 5G offers continue to hold it back. The Rs.300 Jio Prime membership, introduced in August, protects users from tariff hikes until 5 September 2027, and analysts expect it to have given some extra revenue support during the quarter.

Now back to the trading floor, because the debut had a few more surprises. Here's the oddly beautiful bit. Of every 100 Jio shares traded on day one, 71 were actually delivered, a sign that people were buying to keep, not to flip. One veteran market watcher put it neatly: those who got shares in the IPO don't want to sell, and those who missed out are chasing it. Two forces, one direction. That's what holds a price up.

A thin free float helped, too. With no promoter selling and only a sliver of the company available to trade, there wasn't much stock to go around.

Parent Reliance Industries, meanwhile, fell more than 3%. Analysts call it the classic holding-company discount. Once a subsidiary lists, the market stops stuffing its full value into the parent's price.

Now for the part that makes grown-ups nervous. Investors who missed the IPO borrowed to buy in. About Rs.2,227 crore of broker funding went into Jio on debut day, and 93% of the day's rise in NSE's margin book went to this one stock. Brokers happily offered the leverage once NSE put Jio in its highly liquid category.

Think of it as roughly 3-4% of a day's cash trading in the market, riding on one newcomer. Leverage is a lovely friend on the way up. On the way down, a 5-6% fall can bring real margin pressure.

Thursday offered a small preview of the nerves. Jio dipped about 2.5% to Rs.1,381 as some booked profits, then recovered to close at Rs.1,421.6.

Zoom out. At around Rs.13 trillion, Jio now sits in the same league as telecom giants such as Deutsche Telekom and AT&T, though China Mobile still leads. But Jio's yearly revenue is only about Rs.1.47 trillion, a fraction of what those giants bring in. So what are investors paying for? Not what Jio earns today, but what it could become. One strategist says the market sees Jio as a technology company, not just a telco.

Bharti Airtel Ltd earns better returns on its capital, 19% against Jio's 10.8%, and more per user each month, Rs.264 against Rs.215.6. Jio's trump card is sheer scale. With more than 533 million users, it is the world's second-largest operator in a single country after China Mobile.

Then there's the question of what Jio sells next. Telecom still brings in about 88% of revenue. Analysts want digital services, now just 12%, to become a real growth engine, and Jio says AI, cloud and connected devices are the next frontier.

How does Jio close the gap? Mostly by charging more. Airtel recently dropped its entry-level plan and raised postpaid tariffs. Jio hasn't followed yet. Analysts expect industry-wide hikes of 12-15% in the second half of this fiscal year, and Motilal Oswal is pencilling in a 15% hike for March 2027.

Worth remembering is that Jio's Rs.300 Prime membership, introduced in August, protects members from hikes until 5 September 2027. And new competition is circling, with Starlink exploring a broader mobile service.

So the party was real. The speeches were heartfelt, the numbers were record-breaking, and even a falling market couldn't spoil it. But Wednesday only proved that people want to own Jio. It didn't prove they'll still want to when the excitement fades, and the spreadsheets take over.

That's the story to watch, because the debut was never really the finish line. It was the starting gun. Jio now has to turn a Rs.13 trillion promise into earnings, returns and, eventually, price hikes customers are willing to pay.

Can it? Will tariffs rise in time? And how many of those leveraged bets survive a bad week?

This one has a long way to run.

India is among the world's biggest users of AI. Yet the computing power behind it mostly sits somewhere else. The country generates nearly 20% of the world's data but has just 3% of its data-centre capacity. More than $100 billion is now committed, with campuses rising from Visakhapatnam to Patna. Sounds like a win. But who captures the value, the ones who host AI, or the ones who build it? And these giant data centres are thirsty for power and water too. India may not need the world's biggest model to win. So what's its smarter play?

Bombay House is not backing down. Neither is Noel Tata. His latest nine-page letter, the fifth since the 17 September board meeting, calls the resolution reappointing N. Chandrasekaran "void" and wants every reference to it wiped from the minutes. He also questions the deciding vote and a business link that Mint first reported. Then comes the demand. Noel wants the meeting recording, the minutes and more, and he has given Tata Sons just seven days. Will the board hand them over?

Anup Bagchi got the keys to India's largest private bank on 27 October. The balance sheet is solid. Pretty much everything else needs attention. HDFC Bank's shares have slipped 6% this fiscal year, after falling 16% last fiscal year. The premium it once enjoyed over peers is shrinking. Controversies have piled up, and senior exits are making headlines. So where does a new chief begin? Rebuilding trust is one task. Keeping talent from walking out is another. And then there's the small matter of winning back the growth that made this bank the envy of its rivals.

Satish Patel grew up using the stream behind his Gujarat home. Today, he says, its water isn't fit even for cattle. He blames the solar giant across the water, Waaree Energies Ltd, a poster child of India's clean-energy push.

Mint's investigation, using documents obtained under RTI, found the factory was pulled up six times by the state pollution board in under two years. One notice ordered a shutdown. What exactly did regulators find? And did investors ever hear about it? Waaree didn't respond to Mint's questions. The villagers, meanwhile, are running out of patience.

Look at the Nifty and October seems fine. It's up nearly 2%. Now look under the hood. More stocks are falling than rising. On BSE, 2,709 declined against 2,399 that advanced, the weakest breadth in seven months. Oil near $115, a war that won't end, and stubborn global bond yields are doing the damage, while foreign investors have pulled out about $31 billion this year. The odd thing is, earnings are strong. Mint's analysis shows profits growing at their fastest pace in 10 quarters. So why isn't the market cheering?

India is considering whether AI platforms need a distinct legal definition and regulatory framework, as debates over a standalone AI law intensify. Big Tech firms favour sector-specific rules over broad legislation, arguing that sweeping regulation could stifle innovation. Lawyers, meanwhile, say existing intermediary laws need an overhaul to address AI-generated content and clarify liability. The central issue is whether AI platforms qualify for safe harbour protection, which shields intermediaries from liability for user content. With policymakers divided on the approach, the government is weighing how to balance innovation with safeguards against misuse.

India is stepping up oil palm cultivation to reduce its dependence on imported edible oils, which cost the country $18.3 billion in 2024-25. The National Mission on Edible Oils-Oil Palm, launched in 2021 with a Rs.11,040 crore budget, aims to boost domestic production by 2030-31.

Farmers are drawn by relatively stable, long-term returns, while companies such as Godrej Agrovet and Patanjali Foods are expanding plantations and processing infrastructure. However, reliable irrigation, suitable growing conditions, and higher yields will be crucial to sustaining the expansion and improving farmers' incomes.

China's inflation remains subdued despite rising global energy costs, with consumer prices increasing just 0.9% in September 2026. Strategic oil reserves and growing electric-vehicle adoption offer some protection, but weak domestic demand, a prolonged property slump and industrial overcapacity continue to weigh on prices. Factory-gate inflation has surged to 5%, squeezing manufacturers unable to pass on higher costs. Meanwhile, sluggish retail sales are pushing companies to rely on exports. Cheaper Chinese goods could help contain global inflation, but also threaten manufacturers elsewhere, intensifying competition and trade tensions.

Tata Motors has secured 87.8% of Italian commercial vehicle maker Iveco Group, crossing the 80% threshold needed to take control after a 15-month acquisition process. The next steps include settling the offer, buying out remaining minority shareholders and beginning integration.

Tata plans to refinance €3.875 billion in acquisition debt over 12-18 months. The deal could generate cost savings through shared engineering, sourcing and distribution networks. It will also give Tata greater global scale, strengthening its presence in Europe and the Americas while preserving Iveco's Turin headquarters and meeting commitments on jobs and manufacturing.

India's share of financially distressed companies has declined, with firms classified as stressed or zombie falling to 14.2% in 2025, according to Dun & Bradstreet. Zombie firms, which struggle to generate enough operating profit to cover interest payments for three consecutive years, remain a concern. About 43% of 971 companies classified as zombies between 2015 and 2025 showed full or temporary recovery, while 25% remained zombies. Construction and textiles had the most such firms, while cement, telecom and media saw higher concentrations. Their persistence can crowd out healthier businesses and weaken economic growth.

That's all from us this week. Subscribe to our newsletters and the website for what's in the news and beyond it. Write to us at newsletters@livemint.com.

Areas including Arunachal Pradesh, Coastal Andhra Pradesh, and Kerala may experience heavy rainfall, while thunderstorms accompanied by strong winds are expected in states such as Odisha, Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, Karnataka, and Telangana.

"The maximum and minimum temperatures over Delhi are likely to be in the range of 26 degC to 28 degC and 15 degC to 17 degC respectively," IMD noted

data.title: EVs, CNG and CBG: Why India’s clean mobility transition also needs an agricultural lens
data.description:
India’s clean-mobility debate is usually staged as a contest between machines: batteries against cylinders, electric against CNG. It is the wrong contest. The better question is what vehicle runs on, and where that energy comes from and the answer could lead to the paddy fields of Punjab and Haryana.

Numbers are encouraging but incomplete. Electric vehicles make up about 11 per cent of all vehicle sales in 2026, and nearly 43 per cent of passenger three-wheelers sold in the first seven months of this year were electric. For short, stop-start city trips, the battery is winning. But electric buses were under 5 per cent of sales and heavy trucks just 0.4 per cent.

An electric vehicle is also only as clean as the power that charges it. Coal and lignite supplied about two-thirds of India’s electricity in the July to September quarter of FY 2026, and officials expect coal to provide about half of generation as late as 2035-36.

The life-cycle reality

This is why a recent TERI study on vehicular emission becomes important. It compared petrol, diesel, CNG, electricity and LNG across six vehicle categories over their full life cycles. Electric mobility offered favourable economics for two- and three-wheelers and certain urban uses, while CNG gave a competitive mix of affordability, life-cycle performance and practicality for cars, taxis, buses and several light commercial applications. The life-cycle record of EVs remains sensitive to electricity generation and battery manufacturing. The lesson is not one fuel, but the right fuel for each vehicle.

That is where compressed biogas (CBG) fits in. It is produced by digesting crop residue, dung and organic waste in sealed tanks, making CBG interchangeable with CNG, which can run through the same pipelines and engines. TERI’s earlier assessment found it can be carbon-negative: up to 1.141 kg of CO₂ equivalent avoided per kilometre for a four-wheeler, the result of avoided methane leakage from unmanaged dung and of digestate replacing synthetic fertiliser. The study estimates that blending 20 % CBG into CNG could make the fuel carbon-neutral over its life cycle. Same fact was also highlighted by Niti Aayog in its Net Zero Report for the Transport Sector released in February 2026.

In fact, an earlier NRI report states that a single CBG plant can eliminate 11,000-12,000 kilograms of PM emissions annually, which is equivalent to emission savings from 1.5-1.75 lac EVs or that achieved by removing 25000 older vehicles from the roads.

The agricultural lens matters because of the feedstock issue. Punjab and Haryana together produce about 29 million tonnes of paddy straw, which are sometimes burnt because the window for sowing wheat after the paddy harvest is extremely short. While the official picture on emissions from stubble has improved, tens of millions of tonnes of residue need a permanent, paying destination, that fines and machines cannot supply.

A prize not a penalty

A CBG plant offers farmers a price for straw instead of a penalty for burning it, villages get a local employer and soil a nutrient-rich digestate. While policy has helped in building demand—blending obligations is set at 1 per cent in 2025-26, 3 per cent in 2026-27, 4 per cent in 2027-28 and 5 per cent from 2028-29 yet existing plants are reported to run at only 20 to 60 per cent of capacity, The reason: feedstock is seasonal and collection is fragmented and year-round aggregation of biomass, long-term offtake contracts and simpler clearances would change that.

None of this competes with the electric future. Electrons for two- and three-wheelers and urban fleets, increasingly green gas for heavier, high-mileage vehicles, and the farm as supplier of one and beneficiary of the other. The test is not which technology wins but whether every vehicle runs on the cleanest energy available to it.

India’s mobility transition will not only be decided in showrooms and power stations, but in the fields, by what we do with the straw left behind after harvest.

Although 31 October falls on a Saturday, it is the fifth Saturday of the month. Under the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) banking holiday rules, all scheduled and non-scheduled banks remain closed on the second and fourth Saturdays, while other Saturdays are regular working days unless a separate state-specific holiday has been declared.

Here's what you need to know about bank closures in your city today, 31 October 2026.

Banks in Gujarat will remain closed on 31 October on account of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel's birthday. The holiday is included in the Gujarat government's official bank holiday calendar for 2026.

The Government of Gujarat notified the list of public holidays for banks in the state for 2026 under Notification No. GS/22/2025/JSR/2025/509/GH, dated 27 November 2025.

The notification states: "The Government of Gujarat, in consultation with Reserve Bank of India, Ahmedabad, is pleased to declare the following days to be public holidays for banks in Gujarat during the year 2026."

It specifically lists Saturday, 31 October 2026, as a public holiday for banks on account of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel's birthday.

This means bank branches in Ahmedabad and all parts of Gujarat will remain closed today. The holiday applies to both public-sector and private-sector bank branches in the state, including SBI, HDFC Bank, and ICICI Bank.

According to the RBI holiday calendar, banks will operate normally in Bengaluru, Bhopal, Chandigarh, Chennai, Jaipur, Jammu, Kolkata, Lucknow, Mumbai, New Delhi, Patna, Thiruvananthapuram, etc.

These cities or states do not have a separate bank holiday notified for 31 October 2026. Since the date is the fifth Saturday, the regular second- and fourth-Saturday closure rule does not apply.

Therefore, SBI, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Bank of Baroda, Punjab National Bank, Axis Bank, and other lenders will keep their branches open today, except in Gujarat.

data.title: Ramalinga Raju who went for a ride on a tiger and stopped smiling thereafter
data.description:
New Delhi, Oct. 31 -- In 2008, Ramalinga Raju had the world at his feet. India's IT industry was poised for take-off, following the boost from the turn-of-the-century Y2K scare, which sent global corporations scrambling to Indian vendors for fixes to their software programmes. The threat proved largely a red herring, but the discovery of Indian IT talent was real. India's software exports had soared from $6.3 billion in 2000-01 to $47 billion in 2008-09, and despite the financial crisis, the long-term outlook was bright.

Satyam Computer Services, the company Raju had founded in 1987, was among the front-runners of this boom. It had closed the previous year with reported revenues of Rs.8,473 crore and profits of Rs.1,688 crore, ranking fourth among India's IT services companies. Its 1992 IPO had rewarded shareholders handsomely, with the stock touching a peak of Rs.544 in May 2008.

Then January 2009 dawned, and another familiar story of entrepreneurial ambition collapsing under the weight of corporate deception burst into the open.

Byrraju Ramalinga Raju, from Bhimavaram in coastal Andhra Pradesh, was an unlikely IT czar. Born into an agricultural family, he graduated in commerce before earning an MBA from Ohio University. On returning to India in 1977, he tried his hand at textiles and construction before starting Satyam with his brother-in-law DVS Raju and just 20 employees. The company surged, eventually employing more than 50,000 people and serving blue-chip clients including General Electric, Nestle and Cisco.

Raju was soon the toast of the industry, serving on prominent industry bodies and chairing Nasscom in 2006-07. Meanwhile, his family ventured into real estate and infrastructure, businesses that would become crucial to his downfall.

On 7 January 2009, Raju stunned investors with a confessional letter admitting that Satyam's books had been systematically cooked. They contained thousands of crores in fictitious cash and bank balances, accrued interest and inflated debtors, alongside large hidden liabilities. The reported operating profit for the September 2008 quarter was Rs.649 crore, while the actual figure was just Rs.61 crore. The gap, he admitted, had grown beyond his ability to manage.

In his letter, he captured the trap he had created for himself: "It was like riding a tiger, not knowing how to get off without being eaten."

The immediate trigger was a proposal for Satyam to buy 100% of the family firm Maytas Properties for $1.3 billion and take a 51% stake in Maytas Infrastructure for $300 million. The deal made little strategic sense for Satyam and appeared to offer a way of converting the company's purported cash reserves into tangible assets owned by the promoter family. Raju later acknowledged that the acquisition was a last-ditch attempt to cover fictitious assets with real ones.

The board approved the proposal, but investors reacted furiously to what they saw as a blatant conflict of interest. The deal was withdrawn the next day. Satyam's American depositary receipts plunged, while the backlash was compounded by the World Bank's decision to bar the company from certain business for improper benefits and the departure of independent directors.

The global financial crisis and a deteriorating outlook for IT spending added to the pressure. The final push came when investment bank DSP Merrill Lynch, engaged to explore ways of enhancing shareholder value, flagged financial discrepancies and alerted the market regulator.

The Maytas fiasco did not create the fraud; it exposed the desperation behind it. The Central Bureau of Investigation later uncovered thousands of fabricated invoices, while scrutiny revealed that even Satyam's reported headcount and operating performance had been exaggerated. The company's stock collapsed, wiping out Rs.13,655 crore of shareholder wealth.

Raju resigned on 7 January and was arrested two days later, along with his brother and Satyam managing director, B. Rama Raju. The government dissolved the board and appointed new directors to stabilise the company.

In April 2015, a special CBI court convicted Ramalinga Raju and nine others in the fraud case, sentencing them to seven years' imprisonment. Separately, Sebi imposed a 14-year market ban. The audit partners also faced disciplinary action, even as the independence and oversight of auditors came under scrutiny. Raju was granted bail after his conviction, with his sentence suspended pending appeal. He has since largely withdrawn from public life.

Satyam itself disappeared into the folds of Tech Mahindra, which bought the stricken company following a government-supervised bidding process in 2009. But the Satyam name has become synonymous with corporate fraud.

Had Ramalinga Raju stayed the course with India's IT story, he could have made billions. Instead, he chose to ride a tiger.

For more such stories, read The Enterprising Indian: Stories From India Inc.

data.title: Here's why Granules India shares could see a reaction on Monday
data.description:
Granules India shares will be in focus on Monday (November 2) after the company reported that the US FDA has issued Form 483 to the company's Hyderabad Unit with 11 observations after concluding a GMP inspection at a Hyderabad facility. This confirms the CNBC-TV18 newsbreak. Earlier on October 19, CNBC-TV18 had reported that the US FDA began an audit of Gagillapur. CNBC-TV18 had reached out to Granules for a comment.

CNBC-TV18 Newsbreak Confirmed

In an exchange filing issued on Saturday, October 31, the company said that the United States Food and Drug Administration (USFDA) concluded a current Good Manufacturing Practice inspection of its finished dosage facility at Gagillapur, Hyderabad. The inspection, as mentioned before, concluded with the issuance of Form 483 with a total of 11 observations.

The said inspection was conducted from October 19 to October 30, 2026.

As per the US drug regulator, an FDA Form 483 is issued to a company when an FDA investigator has observed any violations of the Food, Drug and Cosmetic (FD&C) Act and related Acts.

Observations are conducted when, in the investigator's assessment, the conditions or practices noted suggest that any food, drug, device, or cosmetic has been adulterated or is being prepared, packaged, or stored in a manner that could lead to adulteration or pose a health risk.

Company's Reaction

The Telangana-based company said that this was the first USFDA inspection of the facility since the Warning Letter of February 26, 2025, which followed an inspection in August-September 2024.

For its part, the company has claimed that none of the observations was related to data integrity or cross-contamination.

Furthermore, according to Granules, the observations concern the enhancements in investigations, change control, process and equipment qualification, visual-inspection controls and documentation practices.

The company further added that there is no impact on manufacturing or distribution of products from the site. In addition, Granules also added that the company will submit a 'comprehensive' response to the US drug agency within 15 days.

Commenting on the inspection, Dr. Krishna Prasad Chigurupati, Chairman and Managing Director, said: “The inspection progressed constructively, and the observations are of a nature that we believe can be fully addressed through our responses and corrective and preventive actions. Quality is the foundation of everything we do at Granules, and we will continue to engage transparently with the agency.”

Ahead Of Q2 Results

The company will be reporting its results for the second quarter or Q2FY27 on November 2. Ahead of that, when we look at its performance in Q1, the pharma company's Earnings Before Interest, Tax, Depreciation and Amortisation (EBITDA) for the June quarter rose by 37.4% YoY to ₹339 crore from ₹246.5 crore.

The EBITDA margin expanded by over 300 basis points to 23% from 20.3% YoY. Granules India's net profit for the period increased by 60% year-on-year to ₹180 crore from ₹112.60 crore. Revenue grew 22% to ₹1,476 crore from ₹1,210 crore during Q1 of FY26.

Stock Performance

When we look at the performance of the pharma company's stock, the shares of the company closed in the green on Friday, with minimal gains of 0.29%. In this year's trade so far, the stock price has expanded its value by over 35%.

Furthermore, the stock is at over 9% below its 52-week high of ₹923.65 and sitting with a cushion of 58.49% above its 52-week low of ₹529.85. The stock has made major gains over the past week and has closed in the green in 7 out of the last 10 trading sessions.

data.title: Can India afford tax cuts right now?
data.description:
With just about three months to the budget, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman is likely to be swamped with demands for more funds or tax relief. One of the loudest is the clamour for a cut in long-term capital gains tax (LTCG) and securities transaction tax (STT). Stock investors argue that a tax cut will bring back foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) who have yanked out a staggering $32.5 billion from Indian equities this year.

The big question for Sitharaman is whether the exchequer can afford tax cuts amidst rising expenses and ballooning debt.

There's an estimated ₹2.85 lakh crore fiscal hole as subsidy bills surge and tax collections slide, according to ICRA, a Mumbai-based ratings agency. That's more than double the revenue from LTCG in the financial year ended March 2025.

LTCG hike didn't start the FPI sell-off, a cut may not stop it

Indeed, the sell-off in Indian stocks started in the fall of 2024 because Indian stocks had run up too much, too fast, and global investors found them expensive. There were juicy profits to be taken out of India, and the AI trade in other countries offered the investors a relatively lucrative opportunity to put their capital to work. It may offer some pain relief to bleeding portfolios, but the government has other responsibilities too. "The government is cutting expenses elsewhere. Cutting spending on essentials when inflation is rising may be politically costly. Prime Minister Narendra Modi's rivals would have more material to escalate their attacks on the administration.

The country has less than 63 million unique people with investments in mutual funds, according to the August data released by the Association of Mutual Funds in India (AMFI). A much larger base of voters with no investable surplus is reeling from the high cost of food, fuel, and fertilisers.

The government has already seen its tax revenue dip 23% in the first five months of this fiscal year due to duty cuts in petrol and diesel.
